items.followUp: What happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction when all enzyme active sites are occupied?

rubric.why: Explains both what saturation means and its effect on reaction rate.
rubric.description: States that substrate molecules occupy all available enzyme active sites.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying that all active sites are occupied by substrate.

rubric.why: The reaction-rate consequence is included in the definition mark above.
rubric.description: Explains that adding more substrate cannot increase the reaction rate once saturation is reached.
rubric.how: The 2 marks are awarded together for a complete definition; do not award separately.

modelAnswer: Saturation of active sites occurs when substrate molecules occupy all the available active sites of the enzymes.
After this point, adding more substrate does not increase the reaction rate.
Note: Award the 2 marks for the complete definition; the rubric is represented as one 2-mark criterion.

items.followUp: Name one enzyme used in food processing and state its use.

rubric.why: Tests one application of enzymes in food processing.
rubric.description: Gives a correct food-industry use of enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example and use.

rubric.why: Tests one application of enzymes in paper manufacture or recycling.
rubric.description: Gives a correct paper-industry use of enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example and use.

modelAnswer: In the food industry, enzymes are used in cheese making (for example, rennin curdles milk).
In the paper industry, enzymes such as cellulases help process pulp or remove ink from recycled paper.

items.followUp: How does an enzyme change when its substrate binds according to the induced-fit model?

rubric.why: Identifies that the enzyme's active site is not a rigid, permanently matching shape.
rubric.description: States that binding causes a change in the shape of the enzyme or active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the active site's flexibility or shape change.

rubric.why: Explains how the shape change improves substrate binding and supports the model.
rubric.description: Explains that the active site adjusts to fit the substrate, enabling the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking induced fit to substrate binding or catalysis.

modelAnswer: In the induced-fit model, the enzyme's active site is flexible rather than a rigid, pre-shaped cavity.
When the substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it closely, helping catalysis.

items.followUp: Draw and label a small intestine villus, showing its blood capillaries and lacteal.

rubric.why: The villus's characteristic shape and outer lining should be shown.
rubric.description: Draws a finger-like villus with an outer epithelial layer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognizable villus outline and its epithelial covering.

rubric.why: These are the key internal structures required by the labeled diagram.
rubric.description: Correctly shows and labels the blood capillaries and central lacteal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly labeling both structures.

modelAnswer: Draw a long, finger-like projection and label its outer layer “epithelium.”
Inside it, draw a network of small vessels and label it “blood capillaries.”
Draw a larger vessel near the centre and label it “lacteal.”

Schematic:          / epithelium \n                  /             \
                 | capillaries  |
                 |      │       |
                 |   lacteal    |
                  \_____________/

items.followUp: What is leukemia, and how does it affect the normal blood cells?

rubric.why: Identifies leukemia as a cancer affecting blood-forming tissues.
rubric.description: Defines leukemia as cancer of the blood or blood-forming tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Describes the abnormal production of white blood cells and its effect on normal blood formation.
rubric.description: Explains that abnormal white blood cells multiply in the bone marrow and interfere with normal blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cause or effect, such as crowding out normal red blood cells and platelets.

modelAnswer: Leukemia is a cancer of the blood-forming tissues, especially the bone marrow.
The marrow produces large numbers of abnormal white blood cells, which interfere with the production of normal blood cells such as red blood cells and platelets.

items.followUp: Define the endoplasmic reticulum and compare its rough and smooth types.

rubric.why: The definition should identify the ER as an internal membrane network in the cell.
rubric.description: Defines the endoplasmic reticulum as a network of membrane-bound channels or sacs in the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the network and membrane-bound nature.

rubric.why: Rough ER is distinguished by ribosomes and its role in protein synthesis or transport.
rubric.description: Identifies rough ER, its ribosomes, and its role in protein synthesis or transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for ribosomes and 1 mark for a correct function.

rubric.why: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and has functions including lipid synthesis.
rubric.description: Identifies smooth ER, its lack of ribosomes, and a correct function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the absence of ribosomes and 1 mark for a correct function.

modelAnswer: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membrane-bound channels and sacs in the cytoplasm.
Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and is involved in protein synthesis and transport.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes and is involved in lipid synthesis.
Diagram: Draw a pair of folded membrane channels; add dots on one section and label it “rough ER (ribosomes).”
Draw a connected smooth section without dots and label it “smooth ER.”

items.followUp: State the main features used to classify organisms into groups.

rubric.why: Defines classification as grouping organisms using shared features and differences.
rubric.description: Defines biological classification as arranging organisms into groups based on similarities and differences.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Cell type is a basic feature used to distinguish major organism groups.
rubric.description: Gives cell type or prokaryotic/eukaryotic organization as a basis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this basis.

rubric.why: The number of cells distinguishes important groups of organisms.
rubric.description: Gives the number of cells or unicellular/multicellular organization as a basis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this basis.

rubric.why: Nutrition, reproduction, or evolutionary relationships are further classification features.
rubric.description: Gives another valid basis for classification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid additional basis.

modelAnswer: Classification is the systematic arrangement of organisms into groups based on their similarities and differences.
Its bases include cell type, such as prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
It also uses the number of cells, such as unicellular or multicellular organization.
Other bases include mode of nutrition, reproduction, and evolutionary relationships.

items.followUp: Explain the three main stages of the Calvin cycle and show how carbon dioxide is used to make carbohydrate.

rubric.why: Defines the dark reaction and identifies where it occurs or its dependence on light.
rubric.description: States that the dark reaction is the light-independent stage of photosynthesis, occurring in the chloroplast stroma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition or location.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide must be fixed to a five-carbon acceptor and form PGA.
rubric.description: Describes carbon fixation: carbon dioxide combines with RuBP and forms PGA.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixation step and its products.

rubric.why: The reduction stage uses products of the light reaction to form PGAL.
rubric.description: Explains that PGA is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the reduction step.

rubric.why: Some PGAL leaves the cycle to form carbohydrate.
rubric.description: States that some PGAL is used to make glucose or another carbohydrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the carbohydrate product.

rubric.why: Regeneration of the carbon dioxide acceptor completes the cycle.
rubric.description: Shows that remaining PGAL is used to regenerate RuBP and completes a cycle diagram.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the regeneration step and a clear cyclic sequence.

modelAnswer: The dark reaction is the light-independent stage of photosynthesis; it occurs in the chloroplast stroma and uses ATP and NADPH from the light reaction.
Carbon fixation: CO₂ combines with the five-carbon acceptor RuBP, forming PGA.
Reduction: ATP and NADPH are used to convert PGA into PGAL.
Some PGAL leaves the cycle and is used to make glucose; the remaining PGAL regenerates RuBP.
Cycle: CO₂ + RuBP → PGA → PGAL → glucose (some PGAL); remaining PGAL → RuBP → cycle continues.
